    ## One thing needed fixing between your commit and green — and it was mine

    Your three fixes were right, but the first run after them was **11/12**:
  02's `R9 mulligan` failed with `expected undefined to equal 'p2'` on
  `mid.pending?.player`. The root cause was my file, not yours.
  `e2e/support/types.ts` declared `pending` as `{id?, choiceId?, kind?,
  player?}` — and `player` is the **networked** spelling only. A hotseat handle
  hands over the raw `GameState`, where `PendingChoice` spells the seat
  **`playerId`** (`packages/engine/src/state.ts`). So your assertion
  type-checked and read `undefined` at run time. Your note that "the support
  type spells it `pending.player`" was accurate about the type; the type was
  wrong about the engine.

    Two changes, both verified:
    - `e2e/support/types.ts` — `pending` now carries **both** names, documented
  as two shapes behind one handle (hotseat = raw `PendingChoice.playerId`;
  networked = `viewDerivedState.player`). This is the real finding: an optional
  field that exists under one name silently passes type-checking and fails at
  run time.
    - `e2e/cypress/e2e/02-prompts.cy.ts:190` — `pending?.player` →
  `pending?.playerId`, with the reason in a comment. I did touch a spec line
  here, deliberately, and I want you to know why I judged it differently from
  the four frozen defects: this line did not exist in the frozen spec, you wrote
  it hours ago, and it is a one-word typo against the runtime caused by my
  wrong type. There is no judgement call in it — `player` does not exist on a
  hotseat `pending`. Revert it if you disagree; 02 goes back to 9/10.

    **M8 — "all twelve specs green in CI on Chrome and Electron": SATISFIED
  LOCALLY ON BOTH BROWSERS; NOT YET IN CI.** I ran both, separately, and said
  which. But `.github/workflows/ci.yml` as committed **cannot pass**, for two
  reasons I measured rather than inferred:

    1. **`pnpm build` is a production build, and a production build deletes the
  dev handle.** `apps/web/package.json` `build` is bare `vite build`, so `MODE
  === "production"`, and both `routes/dev/hotseat.tsx:28` and `game/net.ts:62`
  gate the handle on `import.meta.env.MODE !== "production"`. Measured: `vite
  build` → **0** occurrences of `__jackioh` in the bundle; `vite build --mode
  development` → **7**. Every one of the twelve specs reaches `cy.jackioh()`
  (through `cy.seedGame`, `cy.gameState`, or directly), so all twelve would fail
  in CI on the first command. The fix is the flag: `vite build --mode
  development`, and then point `vite preview --outDir` at whatever `--outDir`
  the build used. Nothing in `apps/web/src` reads the `E2E` variable at all, so
  `E2E=1` is not needed for the client side either way.
    2. **The failure-artifact upload collects nothing.** CI uploads
  `e2e/cypress/screenshots` and `e2e/cypress/videos`, but
  `e2e/cypress.config.ts` writes `screenshotsFolder: "artifacts/screenshots"`
  and `videosFolder: "artifacts/videos"` — so the paths are `e2e/artifacts/…`.
  `e2e/cypress/screenshots` does not exist. With `if-no-files-found: ignore`
  this fails silently, which is the worst kind: a red CI run with no evidence
  attached. Note `video: false` in the config too, so the videos path is empty
  regardless unless CI overrides it.

    Everything else in that workflow is right, and better than what I would have
  written: one job per browser so Chrome and Electron cannot mask each other, a
  fresh runner per browser (stronger than my restart-in-one-job),
  `/api/catalog` as the readiness probe, `retries` left alone rather than raised
  to paper over red, and BUILD §5's items run individually instead of hidden

    ## Where I pushed hardest — what the tests actually do

    **T1 timing (the one you flagged).** It is real, not weaker than advertised.
  It runs `50 × 3 = 150` redemptions **interleaved**, a fresh profile and IP
  per sample (so the 5/h and 20/h limiters don't divert samples into a different
  branch), asserts `response.status === 400` on every one so all three are
  genuinely the step-5 refusal, then `expect(all).toHaveLength(150)` and `max −
  min ≤ 5`. It also carries two anti-vacuity controls the codebase's earlier
  failures would have needed: it asserts the *underlying* work per kind was
  lopsided by **more than** 5 ms and **less than** the 250 ms floor, so the flat
  result is attributable to the padding rather than to a coincidentally uniform
  code path. Remove `padTo` (`/apps/server/src/api/codes.ts:355`) and both the
  spread assertion and `min ≥ REDEMPTION_RESPONSE_FLOOR_MS` fail. **Caveat:** it
  measures a *virtual* clock (`createVirtualTimers`, with the cost model
  injected by the test at `codes.test.ts:480–519`), not wall time. It proves the
  padding logic; it cannot see a timing leak from CPU work that is not routed
  through `timers.charge`.

    **T1 identical error.** Compares the **whole serialized body**
  (`response.text()`, `new Set(bodies).size === 1`) plus status, and pins the
  exact bytes to
  `{"error":{"code":"invalid_code","message":REDEMPTION_IDENTICAL_ERROR}}`. Not
  a status-code-only assertion.

    **T1 pending 403 — all three?** Yes, but not uniformly. Collection and
  loadout (GET **and** PUT) are exercised against the **real** route factories.
  Queue is exercised only on `DELETE /api/queue` (`queue.test.ts:366`); **`POST
  /api/queue` is declared `auth: "active"` at
  `/apps/server/src/api/queue.ts:380` but no test asserts a pending account gets
  403 from it.** Separately, `/apps/server/test/api/codes.test.ts:748` ("403s a
  pending account on an `active` route while letting it redeem") is *not*
  evidence for the three endpoints — it builds a **stand-in** `/api/collection`
  route inline and says so in its own comment. The real coverage is the three
  files above.

    **T2 fault injection.** It genuinely injects. `deps.store.onCall` throws
  between the two writes, tested **both ways round**, and `:83` adds the mirror
  control (a pre-existing row must also roll back), which is exactly the
  assertion that would catch a happy-path-only test. Not the happy path.

    **T4 hidden information (CLAUDE.md rule 7).** This is a **protocol-level**
  test over real serialized frames: `FakeSocket.sent` is a `string[]` of exactly
  what the actor passed to `socket.send()`, and the test does
  `JSON.parse(frame)` and walks every key/value of every frame both sockets
  received (`actor.test.ts:372–378`). It builds **disjoint** decks
  (`p1-secret-*` / `p2-secret-*`) specifically so the scan cannot pass for the
  wrong reason, asserts both hands are non-empty first, drives the match without
  playing anything so nothing becomes legitimately public, and additionally
  scans for `GameState`-only keys (`library`, `hands`, `seed`, `rngCursor`,
  `pendingChoice`, …). It would fail on a regression that broadcast the wrong
  seat's view or a raw state frame.

    **T4 recovery.** Deep-equals the **full** `viewFor` for both seats before
  and after `registry.stop()` + reattach (`toEqual(before.p1)` /
  `toEqual(before.p2)`), crashes mid-*prompt*, drives the **real** clock so
  `clockMs` is a live field, compares `engine.hashState`, and proves the nonce
  map was rebuilt from the log (retrying `n3` returns `seq: 3` with no fifth
  row).

    ### The two findings that matter

    **T1 layout overflow — PARTIAL, and the test says so itself.**
  `Board.test.tsx:68-72` states plainly that jsdom has no layout engine, that
  `document.body.scrollWidth` is always 0 there, that asserting on it "would be
  a fake pass", and that "the real pixel check at 1280x720 and 390x844 is the
  Cypress spec's job (BUILD M8)". It *does* loop over both viewports via
  `setViewport()`, but I grepped all of `apps/web/src/game/*.ts{,x}`: the only
  references to `innerWidth`/`innerHeight`/`matchMedia`/`resize` outside the
  test itself are in `animations.ts:480-483`. No board component reads the
  viewport, and vitest stubs CSS imports so `board.css`'s `@media (max-width:
  760px)` never applies — so both iterations render an **identical DOM**, and
  the viewport loop is decorative. The per-element `getComputedStyle` scan at
  `:89-97` is therefore near-vacuous (nothing but the DEF `rotate(90deg)` inline
  style exists to inspect). What actually has teeth is the static text scan of
  `board.css` at `:102-105` — `grid-template-columns: repeat(5, minmax(0, 1fr))`
  plus `max(declared px widths) <= 390` — and both mutations confirm it bites.
  So the item is honestly a CSS-declaration ceiling check, not a
  rendered-overflow check. The hidden-information half of the same acceptance
  line is fully proved and mutation-tight.

    **T3 — the vitest half does not exist.** `hotseat.test.ts:223` runs **two
  `createHotseat` sessions in the same vitest process against a scripted fake
  engine** (`makeEngine()` at `:46`) whose `reduce` just increments a turn
  counter and whose `hashState` is `JSON.stringify` of `{turn, active,
  pendingFor}` (`:132`). The file's own header (`:4-7`) says so:
  "`packages/engine` does not compile yet, so there is no engine to test the
  session against — and there should not be one here anyway: what M5-T3 owns is
  the LOOP". It is a determinism check on the session wrapper (nonces, log,
  seat) and would pass against an arbitrarily nondeterministic engine.
  Confirming there is no other route in vitest: only `engine.real.ts` imports
  `@jackioh/engine` in `apps/web` and it is behind a lazy dynamic import,
  `apps/web/src/routes/dev/` contains only `hotseat.tsx` with **no test file at
  all** (so the URL params, seat-switch button and `window.__jackioh` exposure
  are untested in vitest), and nothing anywhere reads
  `e2e/artifacts/01-hotseat-full-game.json` (keys are exactly
  `['seed','decks','log']`, 29 actions, **no hash**).

    The real cross-check does exist — but entirely inside Cypress, i.e. inside
  the very gate being measured separately:
  `e2e/cypress/e2e/01-hotseat-full-game.cy.ts:211` →
  `e2e/support/commands.ts:808` `replayCheck` → `e2e/support/tasks/replay.ts:35`
  → `e2e/support/tasks/replay-runner.ts`. That runner *is* a genuine
  independent fold, not a self-comparison: it spawns a Node child under `tsx`,
  registers the card scripts, calls `fold({seed, decks, log, catalog})` from
  `packages/engine/src/replay.ts` **from scratch**, and compares
  `hashState(foldedState)` against `hashState(browserFinalState)`.
  `e2e/support/tasks/replay.ts:10` even concedes the missing half: "The recorded
  log is also written to e2e/artifacts/<label>.json so the engine team can add
  a literal vitest replay over it later." That literal vitest replay has not
  been added. `packages/engine/test/replay-scripted.test.ts:372` folds 30
  scripted games to identical hashes, but its decks are engine-internal fixtures
  and it never sees a browser-produced log.

    ### T4 event-count check, both directions

    1. **Spec 09, "a card dragged into a second deck is refused" — ABSENT as

  animating. The header concedes this at `:306-309`. Nothing here would catch an
  AI turn whose intermediate actions were applied without ever entering the

  WEAKER-THAN-STATED.** "Shown" is proved as a URL redirect (`:230`, `:233`) and
  an API read; the screen's contents are never asserted. The bad-code error is
  asserted on `POST /api/codes/redeem` responses, never on the

  genuinely absent from `e2e/support/testids.ts`.

    ## 5. Runtime

    - `sh apps/server/test/sql/run.sh`, cold container, image already local:
  **2.2–2.4 s**, reproducible across five runs.
    - `pnpm test:sql`: **~8.4 s** on this machine — about 6 s of that is
  pnpm/node startup, not the suite.
    - Add a one-time `docker pull postgres:16` (159 MB) on a runner without a
  warm cache; typically 10–25 s on GitHub-hosted runners.

    ## 6. What the CI job needs

    **Do not use a `services:` block.** `run.sh` starts and manages its own
  container via `docker run` / `docker exec` and never speaks TCP to Postgres,
  so an Actions service container would be started, ignored, and the suite would
  still spin up its own. What it needs is a runner with a Docker daemon it can
  drive.

    - **Runner**: `ubuntu-latest` (or any self-hosted runner where the job can
  run `docker`). GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runners have Docker on PATH, so nothing
  extra is required. macOS runners do **not** — avoid them for this job.
    - **Image**: `postgres:16`, pulled by the script itself. Optionally pre-pull
  with `docker pull postgres:16` as a step so the pull time shows separately
  from the test.
    - **Service config**: none.
    - **Environment**: none. No `DATABASE_URL`, no secrets. The script sets
  `POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres` on its own container and connects as the
  `postgres` superuser over `docker exec`. It hardcodes container name
  `jackioh-pg-test`, so don't run two copies of this job concurrently on the
  same self-hosted runner.
    - **Node/pnpm**: only if you invoke it as `pnpm test:sql`. `sh
  apps/server/test/sql/run.sh` needs neither, so on a runner where you haven't
  already done the pnpm setup, calling the script directly is cheaper.
    - **Timeout**: `timeout-minutes: 5` is generous. The suite is ~2.5 s plus
  the image pull.
    - **Cleanup**: the script leaves the container running so a human can
  inspect the database after a failure. On an ephemeral runner that's free; on a
  self-hosted one add `if: always()` → `docker rm -f jackioh-pg-test`.
    - **Gate placement**: this is BUILD M6-T3's raw SQL test (CHECK 14 at
  `01_schema_invariants.sql:626`), so it belongs on the M6 gate. It is
  independent of `pnpm test` — nothing it asserts overlaps the vitest suite,
  which runs against an in-memory fake — so it can run as its own job in
  parallel.

    ## 7. Verification

    - `./node_modules/.bin/eslint .` → exit **0** (it lints neither `.sql` nor
  `.sh`, so the change is inert to it; confirmed rather than assumed).
    - `package.json` parses (`JSON.parse`), `scripts["test:sql"]` reads back
  correctly, and `pnpm test:sql` exits 0.
    - Final clean run: exit 0, 41 `OK` assertions across the three files, `===
  ALL CHECKS RAN ===` and `### ALL LIFECYCLE CHECKS RAN ###` both reached.
    - Container removed; no probe databases left behind. Nothing committed.

    ## 8. Two things left for you

    1. **02 and 03 still report failures with `raise notice 'FAIL …'`** (roughly
  20 sites). They are now caught, but only by the runner's output grep — a
  weaker net than 01's `raise exception`, and it would miss a check that fell
  silent instead of printing. I stayed out of them beyond the ON_ERROR_STOP flag
  since they were not in scope; converting them to the CHECK 12 pattern is the
  obvious follow-up.
    2. **CHECK 4 has no vacuity guard and cannot have one** — `public` holds no
  functions at all, so "no SECURITY DEFINER function in public" is trivially
  true today. It is a regression trap, not a measurement. That is called out in
  a comment at `01_schema_invariants.sql:141` rather than papered over.

⏺ The SQL result is the biggest finding of the session so far.

  A suite that could not fail, and nothing ran it anyway.
  apps/server/test/sql/run.sh applies the four migrations to a real Postgres and
  checks the invariants BUILD M6 depends on — including CHECK 14, which is the
  "raw SQL test" M6-T3's acceptance names by hand. It exited 0 in 2.4s and
  always would have: CHECKs 1–10, 16 and 17 were bare selects, so psql printed
  the answer and moved on whichever way it came out. CHECK 3 printed the unique
  index's definition and compared it to nothing.

  Four more caught the real violation but accepted any error as proof of it.
  CHECK 15 passed when app.assert_catalog_version was deleted outright — the
  function whose absence it existed to detect.

  Three holes the audit hadn't spotted turned up too, and one of them matters a
  great deal: CHECK 9 was eyeballing the identical-error property — §9.4
  requires missing, expired and exhausted invite codes to answer identically,
  which is the entire reason the invite gate exists, and nothing asserted it.

  It now carries 28 raise-exception paths, each proved by breaking the invariant
  against a throwaway database and watching it go red — re-keying the index on
  (profile_id, slot, card_id), granting update to PUBLIC, disabling an
  append-only trigger, making a definer function stop pinning search_path. Two
  of those breaks were invisible to the old queries: information_schema hides
  grants to PUBLIC entirely, so the check was rewritten onto aclexplode.

  Two vacuity guards worth naming: CHECK 1 used to pass on an empty schema, and
  CHECK 5's "no write policy reachable by a client role" is trivially true when
  there are no policies at all — both now fail loudly.

  No migration was touched; they're checksum-locked and append-only, and every
  invariant turned out to be assertable without one. The suite runs in ~4s and
  now has its own CI job, verified against act. Two limitations are recorded
  rather than papered over: specs 02 and 03 still report by raise notice, caught
  only by the runner's output grep, and CHECK 4 has no vacuity guard because
  public holds no functions at all — it's a regression trap, not a measurement.

    # Measurement 1 — SPA fallback under `vite preview`

    Every route the suite touches is served. `curl` against the running preview
  server, `200` with `text/html` and the `<div id="root">` present in each body:

    | Path | Status | Body |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | `/` | 200 text/html | root div |

    | `/login` | 200 text/html | root div |
    | `/invite` | 200 text/html | root div |

    So the deep-link 404 you were worried about does not happen: `vite preview`
  runs in SPA mode and rewrites unknown paths to `index.html`.

    One consequence worth knowing rather than fixing:
  **`/assets/does-not-exist.js` also returns 200 `text/html`**, because the
  catch-all does not exclude the asset directory. A missing or mis-hashed chunk
  therefore arrives as HTML where JavaScript was expected and surfaces as a
  parse error in the console, not as a 404 in the network panel. Nothing in the
  suite depends on it; it is a debugging trap for whoever one day chases a
  chunk-loading failure in CI.

    # One new CI finding — `vite preview` binds IPv6 loopback only

    Measured on this machine, against the running preview server:

    ```
    http://localhost:5173/    -> 200
    http://[::1]:5173/        -> 200
    http://127.0.0.1:5173/    -> 000   (connection refused)
    lsof: node ... TCP [::1]:5173 (LISTEN)        <- IPv6 only
    ```

    The API server is unaffected — `@hono/node-server` binds `*:8787`, and both
  `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` answer 200 there.

    The workflow probes `npx wait-on http://127.0.0.1:5173 …`. On this host that
  URL never answers, so the step would burn its full 120 s and fail with both
  servers healthy. I hit exactly that with my own probe script before switching
  it to `localhost`.

    **I cannot tell you it will fail on ubuntu-latest** — whether
  `listen('localhost')` binds v4, v6 or both is the runner's resolver and Node's
  `autoSelectFamily`, and I have no Linux box here. So treat it as a risk, not
  a certainty. The zero-cost removal of the risk is to probe the URL Cypress
  actually uses: `baseUrl` in `e2e/cypress.config.ts` is
  `http://localhost:5173`, so `wait-on http://localhost:5173` both matches the
  suite and is family-agnostic. Leave the `127.0.0.1:8787` probe alone or change
  it for symmetry; it works either way.

⏺ The second container run paid for itself immediately.

  It went red where the first went green — and on exactly the test I'd flagged
  as a risk two hours ago and chosen to leave alone. reduce.test.ts:104, Test 
  timed out in 5000ms. Not an assertion; the same test passed in that same job's
  own unit step minutes earlier.

  The 5 seconds was never chosen for it — it's vitest's inherited default, and
  it's the only thing in that file measuring the machine rather than the engine.
  Measured: the whole file runs in 704ms, or 1.00s under coverage
  instrumentation. So a sub-second test carrying about 5× headroom, while pnpm 
  test:coverage instruments every module the walk touches and a 2-core shared
  runner supplies the rest. It had already failed this way once under local
  load; I recorded it as "the note to point at if it fires," and it fired.

  Now 30s with those measurements written beside it. No assertion changed — the
  walk still probes every action legalActions offers at each of the 200 states —
  and I proved the budget still bites by setting it to 1ms and watching the
  test fail.

  Worth being explicit about one thing: I caused that red myself by launching
  three reviewers as the container run started, which is the contention I'd been
  carefully avoiding all session. It was a mistake that happened to be
  productive — it reproduced a real CI failure mode on the runner-like
  environment rather than leaving it as a hypothesis in a report.

    ## Spec 09, `it` by `it`

    ```
    ✓ L1 — a loadout needs exactly three decks
    ```

    The six API assertions are untouched — as you said, the law half is worth

    ## The drag, at the layer BUILD names

    `cy.dragCardToDeck(cardId(1), 1)` — the real gesture, onto deck 2's region.
  Before the drag the pool already marks the card `data-legal="false"` (M5-T2's
  existing vocabulary, not a second word for the same statement) with
  `data-in-deck="1"`. After it: deck 2 never gained the row, deck 1 never lost
  it, both counts still `20`, the pool card carries `data-refused="true"`, and
  `LOADOUT_ERRORS` still reports `data-count="0"` with no `loadout-error-L4` —
  because the refusal is what *kept* the draft legal, which is the difference
  between refusing a drag and reporting L4 afterwards.

    **I added a control, because without one the test was vacuous.** "Refused"
  and "the gesture never fired at all" leave an identical board, so every
  assertion above would have passed against a `dragCardToDeck` that did nothing.
  So the same command then drags a card the loadout does *not* hold onto the
  same region: it lands, deck 2 becomes 21, and the builder renders L2's
  sentence for deck 2. The gesture demonstrably works, and the refusal is
  specific to the card being held elsewhere.

    ## Each of L1–L6 "shown" — what I could reach, and the finding underneath

    L2's rendered sentence is asserted twice against the exact validator string,
  inside `LOADOUT_ERRORS` via `loadoutErrorId("L2")`: once as the client's live
  verdict (`data-source="client"`, no save involved) and once as the server's
  after a refused save (`data-source="server"`). That is §9.3's "the client's
  verdict is UX while the server's is law" shown agreeing word for word — which
  is the point of M6-T3's one shared validator module. The refused save leaves
  storage untouched, which the test also asserts so the next `it` opens a legal
  draft.

    **The other five rules cannot be reached from a browser at all, and that is
  a property of the product rather than a gap in the spec.** The builder's draft
  has exactly two sources — the loadout `GET /api/loadout` returns, which the
  server only ever stored because it was legal, and edits through the UI — and
  the UI refuses to construct five of the six failures:

    - `addCard` (`deckbuilder/loadout.ts`) refuses any card already held in
  **any** deck, so no draft can reach L3's duplicate or L4's
  same-card-in-two-decks. That refusal *is* BUILD's second clause.
    - `poolFrom` excludes Token-tagged cards and anything the collection does
  not hold, so L3's Token branch and L6's unknown id are never draggable.
    - The builder always renders three decks, so L1's wrong count cannot be
  typed in.
    - L5 cannot be isolated anywhere, for the R111 reason the header already
  gave.

    What remains is L2: take a card out and the deck holds 19. So the honest
  reading of BUILD's "each of L1–L6 shows its message" is that only one of the
  six is reachable through a browser; the other five are rendered-message-tested
  at the layer that *can* hand the builder an arbitrary draft —
  `Deckbuilder.test.tsx`, which mounts one and asserts all six against
  `validateLoadout`'s own output. I wrote that reasoning into the header rather
  than leaving the row looking half-satisfied.

    **No product bug surfaced.** I went in expecting one, since a test pointed
  at the wrong layer for this long usually hides something. The builder's
  testids, its two string builders and `e2e/support/testids.ts` agree byte for
  byte, the drag lands and is refused exactly where it should be, and the
  client's sentence matches the server's character for character.

    - **Kept, because they are still correct:** L6's "banned" branch is

  and the boot path works

    **Verification (all re-run after the last edit):** `tsc -p
  apps/server/tsconfig.json` → 0 · `eslint .` → 0 · `vitest run --project
  server` → 281 passed / 18 files (was 241; +40 mine) · `pnpm test:db` → 63

  `apps/server/package.json` and installed.

    ### 1. The `app.*` inventory

    **Called directly by the store (the port's shape fits):**
    | Function | Port method |
    | --- | --- |
    | `app.save_loadout(uuid,text,jsonb)` | `loadouts.replace` — §9.4's "all
  three decks in one transaction or nothing", L1/L2/L3/L5/L6 re-checked in SQL |
    | `app.resolve_deck(uuid,int)` | `loadouts.get` — the same function the
  queue ticket freezes, so a read deck and a frozen deck can't differ |
    | `app.append_match_action(uuid,text,uuid,text,jsonb)` |
  `matches.appendActions` — assigns `seq` from `last_seq` under a row lock,
  dedupes by nonce |
    | `app.claim_ticket_pair(uuid,uuid,uuid)` | `tickets.claimPair` — §9.5's one
  atomic statement |
    | `app.live_matches()` | `matches.live` |
    | `app.redeem_invite_code(uuid,text,text)` | **not a port method** — see §5
  |

    **Reached through them / through triggers, not restated in TypeScript:**
  `app.assert_catalog_version` (inside `save_loadout`), `app.handle_new_user`
  (signup → pending profile), `app.on_profile_activated` →
  `app.grant_launch_collection` → `app.grant_cards` (R111's launch grant, fired
  by `profiles.setStatus(active)`), `app.deny_row_mutation`,
  `app.set_updated_at`, `app.setting`/`app.catalog_version`,
  `app.current_profile_id`/`app.profile_is_active`.

    **Deliberately not called, with reasons:**
    - `app.create_room` / `app.join_room` — both mint the match id themselves
  and set `current_match_id`; the port mints the id in `rooms.claim` and
  `src/match/rooms.ts` sets `setInMatch` only *after* the claim (§9.5's "not in
  a match" would otherwise refuse the host their own room).
    - `app.start_match` — mints the id; `matches.create` receives one.
    - `app.end_match` — it ends the match *and* writes the results row, both
  ratings, both `current_match_id`s and cancels stray tickets.
  `src/api/results.ts` already does all five through `results.insert` /
  `profiles.setRating` / `setInMatch` / `tickets.cancel` / `matches.finish`
  inside one `Store.tx` that my methods join, so the ending is still one
  transaction with the same writes — calling it would do the other four twice.
    - `app.reap_stale_matches` — `reapStuckMatches` in `results.ts` is the
  reaper, via `matches.live()` + its own idempotent write (R112's `turns = 0`,
  ratings unchanged — same policy).
    - `app.grant_cards` — takes *deltas*; `ports.ts` says `upsertQuantities`
  "SETS the absolute value … never `quantity + excluded`" because `grantCards`
  already added the delta inside the same transaction. Calling it would double
  every grant.

    ### 2. RLS / role, applied per request

    `ACTING_ROLE = service_role`. Every method goes through one primitive
  (`Session.run`) that issues `begin` **first**, then one parameterised
  statement — `select set_config('role','service_role',true),
  set_config('request.jwt.claim.sub',$subject,true)` — so `SET LOCAL` can never
  run outside a transaction and silently leave the connection as the owner.
  There is no code path that executes SQL outside a transaction. `subject` is
  the profile the call is about (`auth.uid()` / `app.current_profile_id()`);
  inside `Store.tx` the role is set once and the subject re-stamped per
  statement. Proven, not asserted: `postgres.spec.ts` attaches a trigger on
  `public.code_attempts` that records `current_user`, `current_setting('role')`
  and `auth.uid()` **as the store's own statement sees them** — it reads
  `service_role` / `service_role` / the profile id, and with `max: 1` (same
  physical connection) a second call records `uid = null`, i.e. nothing leaked
  past commit.

    Note: `service_role` carries BYPASSRLS by design (every migration's closing
  summary says so), so this does not change results today — but the server is no
  longer a superuser, so a missing grant or a function not granted to
  `service_role` now fails loudly instead of passing by ownership.

    ### 3. What is real vs. not implemented

    **All 38 methods + `tx` are implemented, and every one has at least one
  assertion against a real database. Nothing throws "not implemented".** The
  shared contract (`test/db/contract.ts`, 38 tests) runs the *same* assertions
  against `src/api/e2e-store.ts` (in `pnpm test`) and against Postgres (in `pnpm
  test:db`) — that pair is the thing that would have caught this gap.
  `postgres.spec.ts` adds 25 database-only tests (role/session probe, the two
  signup/launch triggers, `app.redeem_invite_code` end to end, `save_loadout`'s
  L2/L5/stale-version/not-active refusals, nonce replay, `deny_row_mutation`,
  three real two-at-a-time races, and the boot path).

    Two mappings are unusual enough to flag, both documented at length in the
  file:
    - **Rooms.** There is no `rooms` table and I may not add one — a room is a
  `public.matches` row with `status='open'` (what `app.create_room` makes it).
  `Room.expiresAt` lives in `ceiling_at`, the column 0004 documents as
  meaningless while open, and `rooms.claim` rewrites the row's **primary key**
  to the match id the server minted (nothing references the row at that instant;
  `matches.create` then completes `open → live`).
    - **`tickets.claimPair`.** `tickets.match_id` is an FK into `public.matches`
  and `queue.ts` claims *before* the match exists, so the claim runs with a
  NULL match id and the same transaction then writes a skeleton `open` match row
  from the two tickets' own frozen decks and links both tickets.
  `matches.create` completes that row — one mechanism shared with the room path.
  If the process dies between the two, an `open` row leaks (harmless: the
  reaper only scans `live`, and both players can re-queue).

    ### 4. Proved / not proved against a real database

    **Proved:** the 63 tests above, including `src/index.ts`'s `loadStore`
  actually resolving this module and answering a query — run through **`tsx` in
  a subprocess**, because `loadStore` imports a *variable* specifier (`const
  specifier = "./db/store"`) that vitest's module runner cannot resolve but the
  real runtime can. (`test/db/loadstore-boot.ts`; I verified the failure was a
  vite-node artifact, not a production one.) Also proved: `createPostgresStore`
  refuses `memory://` at construction, so `loadStore` cannot succeed with a
  store that would fail later.

    **Not proved:** anything against a real Supabase project (roles, privileges
  and `auth.users` are stubbed in `test/db/bootstrap.sql` to mirror what
  Supabase grants); behaviour through Supabase's **pooled/PgBouncer** connection
  string (every statement is in an explicit transaction and no named prepared
  statements are used, so it should be fine — untested); any HTTP handler
  against Postgres (the API suite still runs on the fake); the reaper and the
  match actor against Postgres; more than two concurrent callers, and only
  within one process; performance and pool sizing.

    ### 5. The one thing I could not do, and it needs your file

    **SPEC §9.4's redemption cannot go through `app.redeem_invite_code` without
  a change to `apps/server/src/api/ports.ts`.** That function *is* the six-step
  transaction; `Store` has no `redeem` method, and `src/api/codes.ts` makes six
  separate port calls (`getById`, two counts, `findByHash`, `claim`,
  `setStatus`, `logAttempt`) inside `Store.tx`. Those six do commit as **one
  real database transaction** now — that part of §9.4 holds — but the steps are
  orchestrated in TypeScript, and any method here that also called
  `app.redeem_invite_code` would double-log the attempt and double-flip the
  status. So I exposed it as `PostgresStore.redeemInviteCode(...)` (not part of
  `Store`, nothing calls it yet) and tested it against the real database through
  all seven result codes, rate limits included. Adopting it is a `redeem`
  method on the port — the runtime agent's call, and I did not touch that file.

    ### 6. What CI needs (you own the workflow)

    A new job, separate from the hermetic one: Docker available (GitHub's
  `ubuntu-latest` has it), Node ≥ 22.13, `pnpm install`, then **`pnpm
  test:db`**. That is the whole job — `apps/server/test/db/run.sh` starts
  `postgres:16` with port **55433** published (override with `DB_PORT`), applies
  `test/db/bootstrap.sql`, runs the real `src/db/migrate.ts` over the four
  migrations, applies `test/db/grants.sql`, runs vitest, and removes the
  container on exit (`KEEP_DB=1` keeps it). Exit status is the gate. It must
  **not** be folded into `pnpm test`, which stays hermetic — the memory half of
  the contract already runs there.

    ### 7. Follow-ups that need a decision or a migration (I invented no
  R-numbers)

    - **`ports.ts`:** a `Store.redeem` method, so §9.4's transaction is one
  database call.
    - **A future migration** would retire three workarounds: per-player grace
  deadlines (`MatchClocks` has two, `public.matches` has one `grace_deadline_at`
  plus two `*_disconnected_at`, which I currently use to hold the *deadlines*);
  a `reason` column on `code_attempts` (`CodeAttempt.reason` is dropped on
  write); and a `rooms`-shaped home for `Room.expiresAt` instead of
  `ceiling_at`.
    - **Deck order is not preserved** — `loadout_deck_cards` stores (card_id,
  count) and `app.resolve_deck` sorts. The engine's seeded shuffle makes this
  harmless, but the contract compares decks as sets and `ports.ts` does not say
  so.
    - **`tickets.slot`** is `not null` and `Ticket` carries no deck index, so
  every ticket is written with slot 1 (the frozen deck is what travels).
    - **`profiles.create` ignores its `email` argument** (email lives on
  `auth.users`) and requires the managed-auth user to exist first.
    - **Every id must be a uuid.** Fixtures using ids like `"profile-1"` work
  against the fake and cannot work against Postgres; `deps.ids.uuid()` is fine.
    - The full divergence list is in a `KNOWN DIVERGENCES` block at the bottom
  of `apps/server/src/db/store.ts`.

    Notable design points:
    - **No `when others` is ever the proof.** All 16 handlers either re-raise
  (`if sqlerrm like 'FAIL%' then raise`) or raise a named FAIL quoting
  `sqlerrm`/`sqlstate`. Rejections compare `sqlerrm` exactly (`loadout: L2 deck
  1 has 1 cards, expected 20`, `update required`, `app.join_room: cannot join
  your own room`, …); constraint refusals use `GET STACKED DIAGNOSTICS
  constraint_name` (`matches_room_code_open_key`, `tickets_profile_queued_key`,
  `matches_room_code_format_check`).
    - **CHECK 2 is new and is the vacuity guard for CHECKs 3–5.** It seeds 58
  `bulk-NNN` cards (test data, in the test file — no migration touched) so the
  catalog holds 60 non-Token cards, grants them via
  `app.grant_launch_collection`, and saves a real 3 × 20 loadout. A
  `save_loadout` that refuses everything dies here with a named FAIL, so no
  later rejection can be a rejection of all payloads.
    - **CHECK 4 is now honest.** L4's index is unreachable through
  `save_loadout` (see §6); the probe builds CHECK 2's legal loadout with one
  deck-2 card replaced by a deck-1 card, guards that deck 2 still holds 20 cards
  with no intra-deck repeat (so L2/L3 cannot be what fires), and asserts the
  exact L5 message. The heading now points at 01 CHECK 14 for the index proof.
    - Discrimination guards where "true" would otherwise be free:
  `live_matches()` must *exclude* the ended match (CHECK 14); the reaper must
  leave the still-open ABC234 room alone and a second sweep must return 0 (CHECK
  18); R110 asserts both halves — the code reissues **and**
  `matches_room_code_open_key` still refuses a *second open* room; R104 first
  proves a legal code (`ZZZ999`) is accepted, inside an aborted subtransaction;
  R112 uses the hero-death result as a control so "turns 0, no rating move" is
  not a property of every row; R106 asserts the switch exists (`get diagnostics
  row_count = 1`), that it read `true` beforehand, and that the same
  account+code redeems once the breaker closes.
    - psql does not interpolate `:vars` inside `$$…$$`, so ids captured by
  `\gset` are stashed in `mlc.*` GUCs via `set_config(..., false) … \gset` and
  read back with `current_setting`.

    ## 7. What I could not assert without touching a migration

    1. **L4's unique index through `app.save_loadout`.** The function checks L5
  (copies across the loadout vs quantity owned) before it inserts, and R111
  grants exactly one copy, so a cross-deck duplicate is *always* refused by L5
  before `loadout_card_unique` is consulted — SPEC §11 R141 says the same thing
  from the other side. Reaching L4 there would need
  `MAX_COPIES`/`launch_quantity` changed or an ownership top-up that contradicts
  R111/R141. 03 CHECK 4 therefore asserts the exact L5 message and its heading
  points at **01 CHECK 14**, which proves the index by raw SQL exactly as BUILD
  M6-T3 prescribes. (I verified the distinction: raising `launch_quantity` to 5
  makes CHECK 4 go red naming `loadout_card_unique`.)
    2. **CHECK 21's discrimination guard cannot be tripped on its own.** Any
  mutation making every result read `turns = 0` with unmoved ratings fails CHECK
  14 first, and `ON_ERROR_STOP` stops the file there. The guard is sound but
  its only independent proof would require the suite to continue past a failure.
    3. **The `current_user = 'authenticated'` guards** defend against a
  psql-level mistake (`set local role` outside a transaction, which is how 01's
  CHECK 12 used to pass vacuously), not against a schema change, so no database
  mutation can exercise them.
    4. **R107, R108, R109** remain unassertable in SQL — `config.ts` values with
  no database behaviour. Unchanged: 03 still names them only in prose, as

    ## 4. Pixel layout — added, measured, controlled; 10/10 is not reachable and
  here's why

    **Added to `e2e/cypress/e2e/12-rotation-and-swaps.cy.ts`**, at the end of
  its one `it` (twelve files unchanged). `cy.viewport(1280,720)` then
  `cy.viewport(390,844)`; at each: `board` visible, the five cards seat 1 can
  see still visible, and `documentElement.scrollWidth`, `body.scrollWidth`, the
  board's `scrollWidth` and its bounding-box right edge all ≤ the viewport
  width. Wrapped in `cy.document().should()` so a resize relayout retries
  instead of reading a stale frame. It also asserts
  `Cypress.config("viewportWidth"/"Height")` equals the desktop pair, so the
  spec and `cypress.config.ts` cannot drift.

    **Measured values:** `documentElement.scrollWidth` is **exactly 1280** at
  desktop and **exactly 390** at phone. No overflow, and no slack either — the
  assertion is tight.

    **Two liveness controls** (installed, run, reverted), because a layout
  assertion that never executes looks identical to one that passes:
    - desktop inverted → `CONTROL desktop 1280x720: expected 1280 to be above
  1280`
    - phone-only inverted → `CONTROL phone 390x844: expected 390 to be above
  390`

    Both viewport iterations execute; neither is vacuous.

    **The three files really did point at each other**, and I quoted them in the
  spec's header block: `Board.test.tsx` ("jsdom has no layout engine … the real
  pixel check at 1280x720 and 390x844 is the Cypress spec's job"),

  there"). `grep -rn "cy.viewport" e2e/` had **no hits** before this.

    **On the 10-unit / 10-backrow board: not reachable, and it is a fixture
  problem, not a laziness problem.** BUILD M5-T1's acceptance names a *snapshot
  test* with that fixture, and `Board.test.tsx`'s `fullBoardView()` **is** that
  fixture (a sibling test asserts 20 drawn cards) — but jsdom cannot measure it,

  an e2e spec the board must be *played* into existence: `/dev/hotseat` exposes
  `{state, seed, seat, log, decks, dispatch, view, legal, hash, setSeat}` and no
  state injection. Filling ten backrow zones needs five settable backrow cards

  12's six occupied zones — four units, one readable trap, one face-down back,
  across both sides and both rows, plus both hands, both heroes, control bar and
  log — is the fullest board the twelve build. I measured that, and asserted
  the premise by name (the five instance ids) so an edit that empties the board
  fails rather than quietly measuring an empty grid.

    **What 10/10 would need, cheapest first:**

  `e2e/cypress.config.ts` plus a React mount adapter, rendering the existing

  a spec change — which is why I did not do it unasked.
    2. A new seeded fixture pair with five backrow-capable cards and five cheap
  units per seat plus a ~20-play sequence inside R2's 30-player-turn cap.

  it.

    Done. `apps/server/src/api/codes.ts` now makes one store call for SPEC
  §9.4's redemption, and `app.redeem_invite_code` is what answers it in
  Postgres.

    ## The port shape (`src/api/ports.ts`)

    `redeem` sits on `Store` itself, beside `tx` — not under `CodeStore` —
  because it *is* a transaction and it writes three tables (`profiles`,
  `invite_codes`, `code_attempts`); it is not an operation on the code table.

    ```ts
    redeem: (input: RedeemInviteCodeInput) => Promise<RedeemResult>;

    type RedeemInviteCodeInput = { profileId: string; codeHash: string | null;
  ipHash: string };
    type RedeemResult = "ok" | "not_pending" | "email_unverified"
      | "rate_limited_profile" | "rate_limited_ip" | "circuit_open" |
  "invalid_code";
    ```

    Why exactly this: the SQL function's signature is `(uuid, text, text)
  returns text` and migration 0001 §6 fixes those seven strings. So the port
  takes the three arguments the function takes and returns the seven values it
  returns — no `now`, no limits, no `emailVerified`, no richer outcome object,
  because any of those would be a parameter one implementation had to ignore.
  Two consequences I kept rather than papered over:

    - **`not_pending` collapses "no such profile", "banned" and "already
  active"** — the function decides all three from one `select … for update`.
  R145 requires those three to be *distinct* to the client, so `codes.ts`
  decides them from the profile `resolveCaller` already resolved, before calling
  the store, and treats a `not_pending` coming back as the race it is.
    - **`codeHash: null`** means "the caller already established this string
  could never be a code" (wrong length, or outside R104's alphabet). It travels
  down instead of being refused early because §9.4 logs the attempt (step 4)
  *before* the lookup (step 5): a malformed code has to cost the same
  `code_attempts` row a wrong one does, or it becomes the one cheap probe in an
  endpoint built to make probing expensive. In Postgres it lands as SQL NULL,
  and `where code_hash = null` matches no row — the function needed no change to
  accept it.

    ## Both implementations

    **Postgres** (`src/db/store.ts`): `store.redeem` is one
  `session.query(profileId, "select
  app.redeem_invite_code($1::uuid,$2::text,$3::text)")` inside `buildStore`, so
  it also works on a joined `tx` handle. The returned string goes through
  `toRedeemResult`, which throws if it is not one of the seven — an unknown
  answer is a schema this store was not built against, not something to cast
  past. `PostgresStore.redeemInviteCode` is now just `store.redeem` (kept so
  `test/db/postgres.spec.ts` keeps its name). `RedeemResult` moved to ports and
  is re-exported here.

    **In memory**: one function, `createInMemoryRedeem`, exported from
  `src/api/e2e-store.ts` and used by *both* fakes — the E2E fixture store and
  `test/fakes/store.ts`. It walks §9.4's six steps in SPEC's order through the
  store's own port methods inside one `tx`, so R111's launch-grant trigger on
  `setStatus` and `codes.claim`'s single-shot guarantee take part exactly as for
  any other caller, and `onCall` charges each step. Two pieces of database
  state the port cannot reach became `RedemptionSettings` hooks defaulting to
  `src/config.ts`: `enabled()` (`app.settings.redemption_enabled`) and
  `emailVerified(profileId)` (`auth.users.email_confirmed_at`), plus the three
  §9.4 numbers. `createTestDeps` now settles timers and limits first and hands
  them to the fake store, so `ApiLimits`' redemption fields stay binding on the
  fake path and a virtual-clock test stamps its own time on `code_attempts.at`.

    ## What changed in `codes.ts`

    `resolveCode` and the `Store.tx` block are gone (~95 lines → ~55). The
  handler now: R106 breaker → R145's three account refusals + the R159 email
  check off the token → normalize/hash (or `null`) → **one** `store.redeem` →
  `outcomeFor(result)` → `noteFailure` → `padTo`. The six port calls became one.
  Externally identical: byte-identical `invalid_code` body,
  409/403/403/429/503/200 unchanged, the R107 floor still measured from the
  handler's first line, R106 still per-router with one alert per opening, the
  attempt log still skipped for rate-limited and pre-store refusals and still
  carries the granular operator reason (`missing`, `revoked`, `expired`,
  `exhausted`, `malformed`, `redeemed`) on the fake. `circuit_open` is new to
  the response mapping — the database's own switch now also produces the 503 the
  server's breaker produces.

    ## The contract (`test/db/contract.ts`)

    A `redeem (SPEC §9.4)` block, nine tests, run against both stores. It covers
  every result code the port declares: `ok` (status flips, one use consumed,
  attempt logged, R111 grant present), `invalid_code` for all five flavours in
  one loop with per-case assertions that the account stays pending and the
  attempt *is* logged, `not_pending`, `email_unverified` (both ways round),
  `rate_limited_profile` (and that a rate-limited attempt logs nothing, so the
  window drains), `rate_limited_ip`, `circuit_open` (refused, code unspent,
  attempt logged, then works again), single-use exclusivity, and R161's
  multi-use exhaustion. `StoreHarness` gained `setEmailVerified` and
  `setRedemptionEnabled`; the Postgres side drives
  `auth.users.email_confirmed_at` and `app.settings`, and `reset()` restores the
  switch.

    ## Things §9.4 does not specify, that this surfaced

    1. **The config knob for the attempt limits stops binding in production.**
  `app.redeem_invite_code` writes §9.4's `5`, `20` and `interval '1 hour'` into
  its own body, and the migrations are checksum-locked, so it cannot be made to
  read `ApiLimits`. `defaultLimits()` fills those fields from the same
  `src/config.ts` constants, so the values agree today and there is no env
  override to disagree — but changing one for a real deployment now means a new
  migration, not `src/config.ts`. Written up in `KNOWN DIVERGENCES (redemption
  limits)`. Worth a ruling if you want the numbers tunable.
    2. **Two circuit breakers, and §9.4 describes one.** The server's R106
  breaker alerts, backs `GET /api/codes/status` and is checked before the store;
  the SQL function has its own switch *and* its own failure counter on the same
  R106 numbers. The fakes implement the switch and deliberately not the counter
  — a fake that counted would open during BUILD M6-T1's 150-sample timing test,
  whose premise is 150 uninterrupted failures. §9.4 says "a global circuit
  breaker", singular, and does not say where it lives.
    3. **§9.4 never says the attempt reason exists.** `CodeAttempt.reason` is
  ports.ts's invention and `public.code_attempts` has no column for it, so the
  fake records `malformed` vs `missing` and Postgres records neither. That is
  why `redeem` returns a result code and not a reason: the granularity the fake
  can keep is granularity Postgres cannot. `codes.test.ts` asserts the fake's
  reason in two places — those assertions are about the fixture, not about §9.4.
    4. **A vanished profile row now answers 409, not 401.** `redeemCode` used to
  re-read the profile and return `unauthorized` when it was gone; now
  `redeemForRequest`'s `profile === null` guard covers the ordinary case and a
  row that disappears between `resolveCaller` and the store comes back as
  `not_pending` → conflict. No test covers it and §9.4 does not name the case;
  say the word if you'd rather it stayed 401 and I'll thread it through.
    5. **R145's list is one short.** `R145` enumerates missing, revoked,
  expired, exhausted and malformed as the code-dependent refusals.
  `circuit_open` is now reachable from the store as well as from the server, and
  both answer 503 with the same non-identical message — which is right (it
  depends on the service, not the code), but the R-row does not mention it.

    ### 2. What I mounted, and why

    **`Game` wrapped in `<div className="app-shell">`** — not bare `Board`.

    `Board` is never rendered outside `Game`, and `Game` is never rendered
  outside `.app-shell` (both `routes/dev/hotseat.tsx` and `routes/match.tsx` do
  exactly that). `.app-shell` has `padding: 12px`, so the real board always gets
  **viewport minus 24px**. Mounting `Board` bare hands it 24px it never has — a
  board overflowing the phone by 20px would have measured as fitting, and the
  item would have been "closed" by a test more generous than the product. The
  mount is the narrowest honest container the board is ever given.

    Left out deliberately: the per-route headers (`.match-bar`, `.hotseat-bar`).
  They are siblings in a flex **column** — vertical cost only, no horizontal
  budget — and including one would make a red run an argument about whose bug it
  is.

    The support file imports `apps/web/src/index.css` (the app's only global
  stylesheet: tokens, `box-sizing` reset, `body{margin:0}`), and the index page
  reproduces `#root`'s one rule and the app's `width=device-width` viewport
  meta, adding no padding of its own.

    ### 3. Measured numbers (Electron 146 and Chrome 153, identical to the
  pixel)

    | viewport | document.scrollWidth | body.scrollWidth | board.scrollWidth |
  board right edge | board width |
    |---|---|---|---|---|---|
    | desktop 1280×720 | **1280** | **1280** | **1256** | **1268** | 1256 |
    | phone 390×844 | **390** | **390** | **366** | **378** | 366 |

    1256 / 366 = viewport − `.app-shell`'s 24px. The board needs exactly the
  room it has; nothing spills. All 20 field cards (10 units + 10 backrow) render
  and each is individually visible at both sizes.

    ### 4. The failure proofs (three, all reverted)

    **(a) Inversion, both viewports** — `to.be.at.most` → `to.be.greaterThan` on
  the board's own `scrollWidth`. Red in Electron and reproduced in Chrome:
    ```
    AssertionError: Timed out retrying after 4000ms: the board's contents fit
  desktop 1280x720: expected 1256 to be above 1280
    AssertionError: Timed out retrying after 4000ms: the board's contents fit
  phone 390x844: expected 366 to be above 390
    ```
    **(b) Sensitivity** — a stylesheet with `.field { min-width: 1600px }`
  appended to the mounted document (no edit to `apps/web`), red at both sizes:
    ```
    AssertionError: Timed out retrying after 4000ms: the document fits desktop
  1280x720: expected 1620 to be at most 1280
    AssertionError: Timed out retrying after 4000ms: the document fits phone
  390x844: expected 1618 to be at most 390
    ```
    This also **disproved a worry I had written into the spec**: `body {
  overflow-x: hidden }` does not clip the overflow out of
  `documentElement.scrollWidth`. I corrected the comment to say what was
  measured.

    **(c) The control probed too — and it was fake.** My first draft asserted
  `cy.get(FIELD_CARDS).should("have.length", 20).and("be.visible")`. With
  `.field .lane[data-lane="5"] .card { display: none }` injected — **four of the
  twenty cards gone — the spec stayed GREEN**, and only went red when all
  twenty were hidden: Cypress's collection form inherits jQuery `:visible`,
  which is satisfied by *any* matching element. Rewritten as `.each(($card) =>
  cy.wrap($card).should("be.visible"))`, the same probe now fails:
    ```
    AssertionError: Timed out retrying after 4000ms: expected
  '<div.card.card-back.card-backrow>' to be 'visible'
    ```
    That is a twelfth check of the kind this repo keeps finding, caught before
  it shipped. **Worth knowing repo-wide: any `.should("be.visible")` on a
  multi-element subject in the twelve e2e specs is an "at least one" check, not
  an "all" check.**

  do (nothing). Both implementations agree — `createInMemoryRedeem` returns

  returns `'not_pending'` before its `insert into public.code_attempts`. The two

  banned and for already-active, so R170's test now reads as the third member of

    ## 2. Your row, clause by clause

    **Correct, and worth keeping exactly as written:** the ruling itself (409,
  not 401), and the reason — "the caller's token was valid and was verified, so
  nothing about their authorization failed; what changed is the state the
  request was about". That is the argument, and I would not improve it.

    **Wrong:** *"The race is only reachable where the redemption is one database
  call, because that is the first arrangement in which the caller is read
  outside the transaction that acts on them; the six-step TypeScript version
  re-read the profile inside it and answered 401."*

    Two things are off:

    - The caller has **always** been read outside the transaction.
  `resolveCaller` (`src/api/http.ts:245`) verifies the token and reads — or
  creates — the profile before any handler runs, in both arrangements. The
  six-step version then re-read it *again* inside the transaction; the outside
  read never went away.
    - So the race was always reachable, and was always caught. The six-step
  version's `if (profile === null) return unauthorized` branch existed *because*
  the row could vanish between the two reads. What changed is not reachability
  but **who can name it**: the re-read now happens inside
  `app.redeem_invite_code`'s `select … for update`, which answers `not_pending`
  for a missing row, a banned row and an active row alike. The server can no
  longer tell the three apart, so it needs one answer for all of them — and that
  is the decision R170 is actually making.

    That reframing makes the row stronger, not weaker: 409 stops being a
  preference and becomes forced. One result code has to cover three cases;
  concurrent activation overwhelmingly dominates the three; and 401 is already
  owned one layer earlier, by `verifyAccessToken`, which returns null for a user
  the auth server says is gone. A handler answering 401 *after* authorization
  has passed is answering a question that was already asked and settled.

    Suggested replacement for that sentence, yours to take or leave:

    > The race predates this arrangement — `resolveCaller` has always read the
  profile before the transaction, and the six-step version re-read it inside and
  could answer "no such profile" itself with a 401. What one database call
  changes is that the re-read now happens inside `app.redeem_invite_code`, whose
  `select … for update` returns `not_pending` for a missing row, a banned row
  and an already-active one alike, so the three become one answer and the server
  must pick what it says. It says conflict.

    **Too strong:** *"Practically unreachable — nothing deletes a profile row."*
  Something does. `public.profiles.id` is `references auth.users(id) **on
  delete cascade**` (migration 0001, line 249), so deleting an auth user — an
  admin action, a GDPR erasure — deletes the profile row. And the holder's token
  can still verify for a window afterwards: `verifyAccessToken` normally asks
  the auth server and returns null when the user is `missing`, but R159's
  positive-email cache short-circuits that lookup for
  `EMAIL_CONFIRMED_CACHE_TTL_MS = 30_000` (`src/api/auth.ts:66, 429`). So there
  is a concrete ~30-second window in which a deleted account's unexpired token
  verifies from cache, `resolveCaller` finds no profile and creates a fresh
  pending one, or finds the doomed one — and the cascade takes it out from under
  the transaction. Rare, not hypothetical. I would say "rare — it takes an
  account deletion inside R159's 30 s confirmation-cache window" rather than
  "nothing deletes a profile row".

    **Probably a slip:** the trailing cross-reference in the amended R145 —
  "from whichever of the two breakers answers it **(R170)**". R170 is the
  vanished-profile ruling and says nothing about breakers; I think you meant
  R106, or no citation at all. The two-breakers observation has no row of its
  own (you noted it for the record), so there is nothing else for it to point
  at. The R145 sentence is otherwise right and matches the code: `outcomeFor`
  maps `circuit_open` to the 503 with `BREAKER_MESSAGE`, never to the identical
  error, whichever breaker produced it.

    (Cosmetic, mentioned only because I cannot edit the file: R170 and the R145
  amendment use `--` where the surrounding §11 rows use `—`.)

    ## 3. On 401 vs 409

    409 is right and I would not change it. The strongest form of the argument
  is the one above: 401 means "I do not know who you are", and by the time the
  handler runs the server does know — a JWKS-verified token, a resolved caller,
  an authorization decision already made and passed. Answering 401 there would
  also be the only path in this endpoint that reports something different about
  the account than every other refusal does, which is the property your row's
  last clause is protecting. And the practical case that dominates the collapsed
  result — a second redemption landing while the first commits — is a conflict
  in the plainest sense.

    One residual wart, not worth a ruling but worth knowing: all three
  `not_pending` cases return the sentence `"This account is already active."`,
  which is false for the vanished-row and concurrent-ban cases. R145 makes the
  *code* load-bearing and the wording free ("a client branches on the `ApiError`
  code and never on the sentence"), so the test asserts `error.code ===
  "conflict"` and not the sentence. Say the word if you want a neutral sentence
  for the shared branch and I will change it.
